# dsh-extra-paths
English | 中文
Let DSH **write to configured external paths on the first try, with no approval** — for the `write`/

`edit` tools and
`bash` subprocesses alike — and, since 0.3.0, **restrict** paths per access level:

`deny` (no read or write), `read`
(read-only), `write` and `always-write`. Paths may be spelled for

Windows, macOS/Linux or WSL, so one configuration can
be shared across machines. The plugin works by

wrapping services (it does not change DSH core) and ships a Web settings
page plus a live preview o
f the effective rules for the current workspace.

## Access levels
Every configured path carries one access level and a set of **surfaces**. `deny` and `read` are new

that every entry was a write grant (`write` / `always-write`, spelled `scope` back

| `access` | fs tools: read | fs tools: write | bash: read | bash: write |

| `deny` | refused | refused | refused¹ | refused¹ |
| `read` | allowed | refused, even inside the w

orkspace | allowed | refused¹ |
| `write` (default) | allowed | allowed while the session is `worksp

ace-write` | allowed | allowed while `workspace-write`² |
| `always-write` | allowed | allowed even
under `read-only` | allowed | allowed even under `read-only`² |
¹ Only where the shell sandbox can subtract permissions: macOS seatbelt and Linux bwrap. On Linux la

ndlock (used when
bwrap is unavailable) and on Windows ACL, bash does not honor `deny`/`read`; the f

s tools still do — see
Known limits. ² The host cannot express extra bash grants on Windows; the fs
tools still grant there.
- **The strictest rule wins**: for one target, `deny` > `read` > `write`/`always-write`. A `read`/`d

eny` rule is never
widened by a broader writable rule that covers it, so a denied subdirectory stays

denied inside a writable root.
`write` and `always-write` merge to `always-write`, and the levels a

re reconciled **per surface**: one root can be
writable for the fs tools while bash may only read it

.
- **`deny` is a hard rule**: it refuses content reads (the `read` tool, image/byte reads, listings

and `watch`) and every
write. The `deny` and `read` rules hold for the fs tools even under `danger-

full-access`; that mode has no shell sandbox
for them to attach to, so `bash` is not covered there.
- **`read` downgrades writes while keeping reads**: use it for directories inside the workspace that

must stay
write-protected (`.git`, `node_modules`, build output).
- **Surfaces** (default `[fs, she

ll]`): `fs` = the fs tools — reads/listings as well as `write`/`edit`/apply-patch and
the delete/mov

e operations; `shell` = `bash` subprocesses. A rule only applies to the surfaces it lists, so an
`fs

`-only `deny` does not stop bash from reading the path (and vice versa).
